lines.note: Ranxi is explained by midare ito, tangled threads; the Portuguese likewise describes entangled threads or lines. The divided empe- continues into çadas on the next physical row.

Çadas completes empeçadas, entangled. The parenthesized material at the far right belongs to the following entry's pertur- rather than this definition; it is preserved in its printed position. Enlargement supports the printed d in dado, although perturbado would be expected; retain this source anomaly rather than silently repairing it to bado.

Midaregocoro identifies ranxin as a disturbed heart or mind. The gloss ends in pertur- and uses the displaced completion printed at the right of the row above; it must not be joined to the next Ranxin entry.
This homonymous ranxin is a disorderly retainer: midaretaru xinca, rather than the troubled mind in the previous entry. Criado mao begins the matching Portuguese description of a bad servant.

Deſordenado completes the description of the retainer as disorderly. The final upright S is the dictionary's written-language label, not part of the Portuguese adjective. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Yurai minamoto identifies an origin or source. The Portuguese gives a beginning or origin; the initial of Principio is read as P, and o- continues into rigem on the following row.
Completes origem dalgũa couſa, the origin of something. The tilde is retained over u in dalgũa rather than expanded or modernized.
The second ranxǒ denotes a disorderly commander, midaruru taixǒ. The visible d in Midaruru corrects the draft's Minaruru; the Portuguese adjective continues below.

runs.text: nado, ou que gouerna mal ſeu exercito, &c.

lines.note: Completes the commander gloss: one who is disorderly or governs his army badly. The scan supports exercito, not the draft's exereito.
Ranxu is excessive, disorderly drinking. The printed Obeber is retained as one word, and the manner adverb is divided after desordena-.
Ranxuni natta describes a drinking occasion becoming disorderly. The Portuguese infinitive Chegar starts its explanation; the article o- is visibly carried to the next row's beberete.

runs.text: beberete a desordem, bebendo todos demaſia-

lines.note: The drinking party reaches disorder because everyone drinks excessively. The final mark divides demaſia-damente; it is not the period supplied by the draft.
Completes demaſiadamente and adds 'without order'. The row closes the excessive-drinking example, not a separate headword.
Xiximurano tadare cuſaru describes flesh becoming ulcerated or rotten. The printed Portuguese begins O es-tar; the draft's er- misread the short s at the line end.

runs.text: tar algũa carne, ou outra couſa ſemelhante co-

lines.note: Completes estar and specifies flesh or another comparable substance. Co- belongs to como on the following row, not a missing Japanese element.
The substance is described as corrupted and shrivelled. Xigaiga begins the Japanese example with the dead body as its subject.

runs.text: Eſta o corpo morto como mur-

lines.note: Ranyexita completes the example of the corpse's decomposition. The Portuguese describes the dead body as withered; its mur- continues into cho below, and no accent is supplied to printed Eſta.
Completes murcho and describes the corpse as shrivelled and corrupt. The adjectives continue the preceding example rather than introducing another sense.
Ranyo is equated with coxi, a carried litter or palanquin. The Portuguese alternatives describe a litter or carrying platform.
Midareta fa identifies scattered leaves. The circumflex in Ranyô distinguishes its printed form from the unmarked Ranyo above; the Portuguese alternative continues below.

The leaves may be carried by the wind. The upright S qualifies the entry's register and is kept outside the italic Portuguese. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Ranza, explained by midare za, denotes a disorderly assembly. The Portuguese describes a gathering of people and divides deſ-ordenada across the rows.
Completes the description of the assembled people as disorderly and disturbed. This is the end of the ranza definition.
Rappu denotes ensemble singing or music involving many voices. The comma after vozes is visible and leads into the instruments on the next row, unlike the draft's full stop.
The ensemble includes instruments. Rappuuo ſuru supplies the verbal example, glossed as performing such music; the abbreviation tilde in Deſcãtar is preserved.
Vſumono aya identifies a kind of fine patterned cloth. The initial Certa corrects the draft's missing e; the tightly printed peçasfinas is retained without silently imposing modern spacing.
Raſſocu denotes wax candles. The two long-s forms are retained as printed rather than regularized to a modern Japanese spelling.
Tçucanu come explains rice not yet pounded or polished. The gloss describes inadequately husked rice; a visible space separates mal from the divided eſ-caſcado.
Completes eſcaſcado and adds that the rice remains to be pounded. Ratriǒno fan is the example of cooked food made from that rice.

runs.text: Comer feito deſte arroz mal pilado.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the preceding food example as a meal made from poorly pounded rice. It is a complete physical continuation of Ratriǒ, not a new entry.
Raxxi is order; raxxiuo midaſu means disturbing that order. The capital O in Ordem replaces the draft's G, and the Portuguese verb continues across the line end.
Completes perturbar a ordem, then introduces an example of speaking without order. The printed Raxximonǒ is retained without separating or regularizing its morphologically awkward sequence.
The Portuguese explains speaking about something without order. Rax- begins the next example, continued in the following row; its terminal division mark is visible.
Together with the preceding Rax-, ximo naicoto describes a disorderly thing. The printed spacing before naicoto is retained rather than supplied from a modern grammatical analysis.

runs.text: Certa doẽça, ou buſtellas cõ q̃ ſe corrom-

lines.note: Rayacu is described as a disease or pustules affecting the private parts. The crop supports buſtellas and an abbreviation mark over q; these replace the draft's malformed buſtllas and unmarked q.

Completes corrompem and locates the disease in the private parts. Enlargement shows a very faint short s after parte, supporting partes; the abraded letter remains a nonblocking caveat. No modern medical identification is imposed on the historical description.

runs.text: Alma, ou eſpirito do que jà morreo.

lines.note: Rei denotes the soul or spirit of someone already dead. The large R belongs with the printed Ei on this row and spans two rows; the draft's Fi and the spurious A on the next row were failures to recognize that single enlarged initial.

This separate rei means reverence or courtesy. Item introduces its additional sense of thanks, continued below; the enlarged letter visible at the left belongs to the preceding entry, not to this text.
The second sense is thanks or words of gratitude. The nasal abbreviation in agradecimẽto is retained, and the following examples illustrate both courtesy and gratitude.
Reiuo ſuru or itaſu means paying respects. The alternative marker l remains unexpanded, while the Portuguese reueren-cia is split at the physical line break.

runs.text: cia como inclinando a cabeça, ou dobrandoſe

lines.note: Completes reverence and explains the action as inclining the head or bowing the body. No terminal hyphen is added after dobrandoſe.
Reiuo yǔ or mǒſu means expressing greetings or thanks. The vowel marks belong to the Japanese verbs, while the Portuguese verb Saudar begins the explanation below.

runs.text: alguem, ou dar lhe as graças.

lines.note: Completes the example as greeting someone or giving that person thanks. The printed separation in dar lhe is retained.

This rei is an established example or custom, explained by tamexi. The vowel after T is abraded; the surviving impression and the ordinary Japanese tamexi support a rather than the draft's o, with the damaged reading kept explicit here.
The custom is ordinary and common. Mainenno reini macaxe refers to following each year's precedent; its Portuguese translation continues at the top of the other column.

runs.text: Conforme ao cuſtume de cada anno.

lines.note: Continues Mainenno reini macaxe from the other column: according to each year's custom. A diagonal scratch damages cuſtume, but the word's remaining strokes and the cross-column example support it; anno replaces the draft's amo.
This rei is a small bell. Reiuo naraſu, alternatively furu, means ringing or shaking it; the scratched naraſu retains enough of its lower strokes to restore the missing r in the draft.
Ru completes furu, the alternative bell-ringing verb. The Portuguese directly glosses ringing the bell.
Tamaxij qi identifies spiritually significant trees. The Portuguese begins a description of renowned or specially designated trees, continued in the following four rows.

runs.text: como as que eſtão junto das varelas, & Miyas

lines.note: These trees stand near temples and shrines. Miyas is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation. The second-pass comparison of its slanted i and single-storey a with nearby roman text confirms italic type; it remains marked for whole-word font review.

runs.text: nas quaes os Camis, & Fotoques entrarão, ou

lines.note: The explanation says that Camis and Fotoques entered those trees. These Japanese divine designations occur inside the Portuguese sentence. Enlarged comparison of their lowercase forms with nearby prose supports italic type, so they remain within the italic span and are also listed as typeface terms.

runs.text: as tem como de ſua mão, per iſſo não he licito a

lines.note: Alternatively, the divine beings hold the trees under their protection or power, so cutting them is not permitted. The crop supports he rather than OCR be; the connective per iſſo is retained in its historical form.
Completes the prohibition: nobody may cut the trees. The object of cortalas is the trees discussed throughout Reibocu.

runs.text: Fotoque que faz milagres, ou couſas,

lines.note: Reibut denotes a Fotoque credited with miracles or extraordinary acts. Fotoque is embedded in the Portuguese definition; the second-pass comparison supports italic type like the following relative clause, rather than roman like the headword.
Those acts cause the Fotoque to be venerated and feared. This row finishes the relative clause begun above.

Reicacu is rendered by the dictionary as unicorn horn. The faint inner letters support vnicorne rather than the draft's vncorne; the historical identification is retained without equating it with a modern zoological species.

Suſamajij ſamuxi explains a cool or cold condition. The second i in Suſamajij is abraded, but the sequence and the parallel form on f415 support restoring it rather than treating the draft's gap as a word boundary.
Fria completes the paired description 'cool and cold'. The short row belongs wholly to Reican.
Tattoi tocoro identifies a precious or venerable place. The Portuguese begins 'place or land', with the qualifying adjectives on the next row.
The place or land is pure and excellent. These adjectives close the first Reichi entry before the homonym concerned with knowledge.

runs.text: Excelẽte ſaber, ou ſaber como de An-

lines.note: This Reichi is excellent or extraordinary knowledge. The comparison to angels is part of the Portuguese gloss, and An- continues into jos below.
Reichi curacarazu means that spiritual or exceptional knowledge is not dark. The Portuguese renders this positively as clear knowledge; Vt is italic and cla- continues below.
Completes claro and adds purity without any darkness. The wording explains the negative Japanese curacarazu rather than adding another example.
Reicon means soul. The repeated tamaxij supplies the Japanese explanation of the compound; the repetition is printed and is not an OCR duplication to delete.
Reifǒ is explained as laws and the order of civil or courteous conduct. Policia is retained in its historical social-order sense rather than read as a modern police institution.
The example says that an exhausted or afflicted populace does not fear the rules of propriety. The omitted opening pilcrow is restored from the crop; Portuguese a- begins afligido below.

runs.text: fligido, & canſado não tem temor de leis, nem

lines.note: Completes afligido: the afflicted and weary people do not fear laws. The visible fl sequence corrects the draft's figido, and nem continues the negative coordination.
Completes the example by saying the people have no regard or obligation toward courtesies. It is the second part of the preceding negative assertion.
Reifô, with a circumflex, denotes precious and excellent things. The visible vowel after ci supports precioſas rather than the draft's precieſas; their restricted display is explained below.

runs.text: não deixão ver, nem moſtrão facilmente.

lines.note: The precious things are not readily allowed to be seen or displayed. This closes Reifô and does not describe the laws in Reifǒ above.

runs.text: Eſtudo, ou exercicio de couſas de-

lines.note: Reigacu concerns study or practice of matters of propriety. Eſtudo and exercicio replace the draft's malformed Eſtido and extreitio; the visible terminal mark after de is retained.

runs.text: policia. ¶ Itẽ, Policia, & arte de muſica.

lines.note: Completes the study-of-propriety gloss, then adds manners and the art of music. Policia remains historical wording rather than being normalized to a modern institution.

The definition names an herb called Acaza and then leaves of grãos. Acaza is a Japanese plant name inside Portuguese prose; its printed italic type is retained and the word is separately identified for optional font review.
Completes the second botanical item as leaves of grãos. The tightly printed degrãos is preserved; this brief gloss is not enough to establish a precise modern botanical equivalence.
Qidocuno xiruxi identifies a miraculous or extraordinary sign. The Portuguese begins 'great miracles', dividing mi-lagres across the rows.
Completes milagres and adds wonders as an alternative. The final upright S is the written-language label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Reigui is explained as matters of rei, propriety or courtesy. The Portuguese equivalents concern polite conduct, not modern policing.
Reijin is equated with gacunin, a performer. The gloss specifies a dancer and player, with the instruments stated on the next row.
Completes the performer's description as a player of musical instruments. It remains a continuation of Reijin.
Tçuneno fi means ordinary days. The Portuguese has plural Dias, not the singular Dia in the draft; the weak final s is supported by the crop and the plural adjective.
Reino fumi identifies a letter of thanks. The Japanese fumi and the visible crossed letter support f rather than the draft's long ſ in ſumi; the Portuguese carta confirms that reading.
Fiyai tocoro means a cold place or part. The Japanese adjective has y, not the draft's j in Fijai; the following molten-metal example makes the contrast explicit.
Quacutǒni reijo naxi says there is no cool place in the heated metal. The pilcrow and the j in reijo are visible; Portuguese po- continues into the next row.

runs.text: ſto no fogo, & derretido não ha lugar, ou cou-

lines.note: Completes poſto no fogo: iron placed in the fire and melted has no cold place or thing. The scan supports derretido, correcting the draft's missing e.
Completes couſa fria and closes the molten-iron example. It is a short continuation of Reijo.

runs.text: Anno ordinario, ou custume de cada

lines.note: Reinen denotes an ordinary year or the custom of each year. The provisional st classification in custume is retained in accordance with the project's ligature convention.
Reinenno gotoxi means as in an ordinary year or as usual each year. The Portuguese anno corrects OCR amno and begins the corresponding customary-comparison gloss.
Completes the comparison as what is customary each year. The different s form in this occurrence of cuſtume is retained rather than made uniform with the preceding entry line.
Reimin is explained by tami, the people or cultivators. The example that follows describes cooking smoke as a sign of their prosperity.

The Japanese begins 'in the people's hearths, the smoke of morning and evening'. The vowel mark in chôxeqino appears circumflex-shaped here; it is retained from the actual type rather than regularized by the expected Japanese vowel history.

runs.text: Na cozinha do pouo, ou laurado-

lines.note: Atçuxi completes the description of abundant smoke. The Portuguese locates it in the kitchen of the people or cultivators, dividing laurado-res at the line end.

runs.text: res pelamenhãa, & à tarde ha grãde fumo q̃ he

lines.note: Completes lauradores and says there is much smoke morning and evening. The crop supports pelamenhãa, à tarde, grãde and q̃ he rather than the garbled draft. Enlargement places the tilde over the first a in menhãa here, unlike the reference sheet's previously audited pattern; that local placement is not normalized. The sentence continues on f415; the separate ſinal de below is a catchword, not an additional body row.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: Anticipates the opening words of f415; not repeated as body text.
